title: Does a Heat Pump Ever Pay for Itself?

generation.notes: Palette: near-black field, off-white type; amber only for the pitch, slate blue for evidence, grey for neutral or advocacy sources, red only for cost added or bills going up. No faces, no logos, no stock footage, no maps. Charts carry only figures from their cited passages; chart notes say what each chart must not imply (modelled, bills vs lifetime, one example group). The Minnesota chart shows dollars of extra cost because the chart units have no 'years'; payback years are on-screen labels from the same passage. The like-for-like baseline is shown as a document excerpt (sc12) so it is seen, not only heard. Render pass: no assets (every scene is drawn by a programmatic renderer from its on-screen text, chart points or excerpt); quote cards carry only the quoted words, with the source named by the citation; diagram scenes render as labelled lines built on the narration (bespoke kinds hp-methods and hp-labels); the fuel table and the dollar chart render as stat tiles (hp-tiles).

scenes.narration: Pitches like these describe payback as if it were a property of the machine. Even an electrification group that promotes heat pumps is more careful, telling readers that "a heat pump will often pay off in about 15 years".

scenes.narration: Over the life of the equipment and without any subsidy, compared with replacing the old equipment like for like when it wears out, 59 percent came out ahead if every home picked its single best option. But no real buyer gets to pick with perfect hindsight, and no single heat pump did that well: the cheapest, minimum-efficiency units came out ahead in 55 percent of homes, and the premium cold-climate units in only 21 percent, because their higher price ate the extra savings.

scenes.narration: Even the most generous lifetime figure here, the 59 percent, is a thin majority, and it assumes every home picks its best option. If only a slim majority of homes come out ahead over the whole life of the equipment, a payback of a few years cannot be the typical case.

scenes.direction: Bars draw left to right; the last bar drops on '$370'.
scenes.narration: A Minnesota study priced a cold-climate heat pump with a propane furnace as backup at $9,450 installed, using a national cost database. Installed while the old furnace and air conditioner still worked, its simple payback came to 14.5 years against an older furnace and 28.8 years against an efficient condensing one, longer than the 18 years the study expects the equipment to last. Installed when both had failed and needed replacing anyway, the extra cost fell to just $370, and the payback to between 0.6 and 1.1 years.

citations.label: RMI, economics of electrifying buildings

scenes.narration: A model of gas-heated homes in Chicago, Providence, Houston and Oakland, at the energy prices it used, found the same pattern. Switching paid off for gas customers who "would otherwise need to replace both a furnace and air conditioner simultaneously". Otherwise, existing gas homes that switched both heating and water heating to electric either paid more for energy, in colder Chicago and Providence, or saved too little to make up the extra cost, in Houston and Oakland.

scenes.narration: Put the pieces together and a pattern appears. If you are leaving propane or electric resistance heat, a heat pump usually pays. Buying when the old equipment is due for replacement is the case the national figures already describe; in the Minnesota example, with a propane furnace as backup, replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together cut the payback from decades to about a year. And if you are tearing out a working gas furnace, the models mostly say it will not pay back on energy savings alone.

scenes.narration: There are things that move these numbers. The first is insulation: for older or leaky homes, Consumer Reports says "it’s always a good idea to first upgrade your insulation and seal any air leaks".

scenes.narration: In one group of homes the national lab model examined, sealing and insulating let the medium- and high-efficiency heat pumps be smaller, cutting their installed cost by $2,500 to $4,000. But the insulation work itself added about $9,000 in that group, so the total upfront cost went up.

scenes.narration: So what should you do with this? If you heat with propane or electric baseboards, you are in the group where the models here found the biggest savings, so getting quotes is worth your time. If your furnace or air conditioner is near the end of its life, that is the moment the extra cost of a heat pump shrinks the most.

scenes.narration: And if both are working fine and you heat with gas, switching early is a worse case than anything these models priced; even at replacement time, the second model found gas homes rarely came out ahead, while the national lab model found most gas homes with central air in warmer climates did. In the model of Chicago, Providence, Houston and Oakland, switching paid off for gas homes that needed a new furnace and air conditioner at the same time, or that paired it with rooftop solar.

scenes.narration: So, does a heat pump pay for itself? For some homes, quickly; for many, never: even when bought at replacement time, one national model found a lifetime gain for 21 percent of all single-family houses, the other for at most 55 percent of homes with any single heat pump.

scenes.narration: Which group you are in depends on the fuel you are leaving, the prices where you live, and whether you buy when your old equipment needs replacing anyway. A quick payback is possible. It just is not a promise anyone can make about your house before looking at it.
